newsitem.title: USA: No US aluminum scrap gap in sight - alloy official.
newsitem.headline: No US aluminum scrap gap in sight - alloy official.

text.p: An aluminum scrap gap in the United States is not expected to occur in the next few years due to an ample reservoir of secondary supply for the castings industry, said Richard Neufeld, president of U.S. Reduction Co, a secondary alloy smelter in Munster, Ind.

"There is no scrap gap now, never has been since 1955, and won't be in the forseeable or even long-term future," Neufeld told an aluminum industry conference, "The Aluminum Scrap Gap", sponsored by Gorham/Intertech Consulting.
A scrap gap is the amount of scrap material not available for those applications intended to be scrap sourced.
"Scrap exists and is above ground. There is enough in the U.S. for the castings industry," Neufeld told Reuters.
He pointed to growth of scrap supply in the U.S. as well as the growing percentage used annually by secondary aluminum smelters and others supplying the casting industry.
In 1995, U.S. scrap supplies stood at 8.2 billion lbs, while secondary smelter use, including exports, was 4.8 billion lbs.
"So we are a consumer of 58 percent of scrap in the U.S., and the primary producers and fabricators use the rest," he said.
Neufeld said that in the U.S., an estimated 10 billion to 12 billion lbs of aluminum scrap will be generated in the year 2000, rising to 13 billion to 15 billion lbs in 2005.
But U.S. secondary smelter use is expected to be 6.0 billion in 2000 and 7.5 billion lbs in 2005.
Neufeld anticipates that more North American scrap will be used by the turn of the century for growing automotive applications.

He expected U.S. demand of just under 6.0 billion lbs of aluminum scrap and primary ingot to be consumed for the production of 16 million North American vehicles projected for the year 2001 compared with about 4.0 billion pounds and 14.2 million vehicles respectively in 1996.
"All in all, there is no worry about available supply of scrap," Neufeld said.
U.S. Reduction uses scrap to produce about 400 million lbs of secondary aluminum for the casting industry.
